nodes.name: systemic risk
nodes.statement: The risk of contagion in the financial sector presents a serious threat for a country's economy. Failure of one particular institution in the financial sector threatens the stability of many other institutions. This situation is called a systemic risk \cite{[23]}.
nodes.statement_short: Systemic risk is the situation in which the failure of one financial institution threatens the stability of many others.
nodes.genus: The risk of contagion in the financial sector
differentia: Failure of one particular institution in the financial sector threatens the stability of many other institutions

nodes.name: contagion
nodes.statement: Contagion, by definition, refers to the idea that any type of financial crisis may spread from one subject (financial institution) to another.
nodes.origin_citation: standard financial terminology; no explicit citation given
differentia: any type of financial crisis may spread from one subject (financial institution) to another

nodes.name: SIR model
nodes.statement: In order to simulate an epidemiological process of such diseases, there is a well-known suitable model, called SIR, which was first introduced in the works of Kermack and McKendrick \cite{[21]}. The model is named SIR for the reason that population is divided into three classes: class $S$ of susceptible, those who are susceptible to the disease; class $I$ of infected, those who are ill/infected; class $R$ of recovered, those who are recovered and have become immune to the disease.
nodes.statement_short: The classical SIR epidemic model, splitting the population into susceptible $S$, infected $I$ and recovered $R$ classes.
differentia: population is divided into three classes: class $S$ of susceptible, those who are susceptible to the disease; class $I$ of infected, those who are ill/infected; class $R$ of recovered, those who are recovered and have become immune to the disease

nodes.name: contagion spreading rate $\beta$
nodes.statement: Parameter $\beta$ denotes the contagion spreading rate. It represents the strength of contagion, where a susceptible bank, that is in contact with a single infected bank, changes its state to infected with probability $\beta$.
differentia: It represents the strength of contagion, where a susceptible bank, that is in contact with a single infected bank, changes its state to infected with probability $\beta$

nodes.name: speed of recovery $\gamma$
nodes.statement: The second parameter, $\gamma$, denotes the speed of recovery. It represents the resistance to contagion. Therefore, an infected bank changes its state to recover with probability $\gamma$.
differentia: It represents the resistance to contagion
an infected bank changes its state to recover with probability $\gamma$

nodes.name: the control $u(\cdot)$
nodes.statement: The control $u(\cdot)$ is a Lebesgue function with values in the compact set $[0, 1]$: $0 \leq u(t) \leq 1$, with $u(t)$ denoting the rate at which assistance will be provided to contagious banks, that is, it is the ratio between the financial support from the Central Bank at time $t$ and the financial needed by the banks at that time.
nodes.statement_short: The control $u(t) \in [0,1]$ is the fraction of a contagious bank's financial need that the Central Bank covers at time $t$.
differentia: with values in the compact set $[0, 1]$: $0 \leq u(t) \leq 1$

$u(t)$ denoting the rate at which assistance will be provided to contagious banks, that is, it is the ratio between the financial support from the Central Bank at time $t$ and the financial needed by the banks at that time

nodes.name: SIR contagion risk model for banks
nodes.statement: The earlier formulated rules of bank transitions from one condition to another lead to the following system of differential equations: \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{dS(t)}{dt} = - \beta S(t) I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dI(t)}{dt} = \beta S(t) I(t) - \gamma I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dR(t)}{dt} = \gamma I(t), \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The three-compartment SIR system of ODEs governing susceptible, infected and recovered banks.

nodes.name: Initial conditions of the SIR bank contagion model
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} S(0) = S_0, \quad I(0) = I_0, \quad R(0) = R_0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Control system of the SIR bank contagion model
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{dS(t)}{dt} = - \beta S(t) I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dI(t)}{dt} = \beta S(t) I(t) - \gamma I(t)-u(t)I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dR(t)}{dt} = \gamma I(t)+u(t)I(t), \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The SIR system augmented with a control term $u(t)I(t)$ moving contagious banks directly into the recovered class.

nodes.name: Transmission and permanent-immunity assumption
nodes.statement: In our work, we assume that contagion can be transmitted from an infected bank to another one, which has not yet been infected, and after recovery the bank produces immunity for a long time.

nodes.name: Homogeneity of banks and constant $\beta$, $\gamma$
nodes.statement: According to the standard SIR methodology, we are assuming that all banks are similar, and both parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are constant for the entire sample. However, in reality, these data are unique for each bank and depend on the force of contagion of the affected bank and the financial stability of the susceptible. Dynamics of the strength of banks is not taken into consideration in the present study.
nodes.statement_short: All banks are treated as identical with constant $\beta$ and $\gamma$; heterogeneity of bank strength is left out of the study.

nodes.name: Constant total number of institutions $N$
nodes.statement: It is assumed that $N$, the number of institutions during the period of time under study, is fixed throughout the contamination time (in our simulations, $N=169$ --- see Section~\ref{s3}). It means that $S(t)+I(t)+R(t) = N$ for all $t\in [0, T]$.
nodes.statement_short: The population of banks is closed: $S(t)+I(t)+R(t)=N$ with $N$ fixed.

nodes.name: Assumption on the initial conditions
nodes.statement: Moreover, we assume that the initial conditions \eqref{eqIC} at the beginning of the period under study satisfy \begin{equation} S(0)\gg I(0)>0 \quad \text{ and } \quad R(0)=0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Contagion and recovery rates taken from the European interbank data of Philippas, Koutelidakis and Leontitsis
nodes.statement: The contagion and recovery propagation rates used in our paper, $\beta$ and $\gamma$, follow the statistics and empirical findings of Philippas, Koutelidakis and Leontitsis \cite{[24]}. The statistical data is taken, with respect to the year 2012, for the 169 largest European banks with total assets over than 10 bn Euro.
nodes.statement_short: $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are taken from 2012 data on the 169 largest European banks with assets above 10 bn Euro.
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data

nodes.name: Initial conditions used in the simulations
nodes.statement: Therefore, using the information that the total number of banking institutions ($N$) is equal to 169, and assuming that only one bank is contagious at the initial time, the values of initial conditions for the SIR model were obtained: $S(0)=168$, $I(0)=1$, and $R(0)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: With $N=169$ and a single initially contagious bank, the simulations start from $S(0)=168$, $I(0)=1$, $R(0)=0$.
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data

nodes.name: Choice of the weight $b = 1.5$
nodes.statement: In our simulations, the initial values of the state variables are given as discussed in Section~\ref{s3}, while the weight $b$, associated with the cost of control measures, is taken to be $1.5$, motivated by the value of possible recapitalization with state funds considered in \cite{[24]}.
nodes.statement_short: The control-cost weight is fixed to $b=1.5$, motivated by recapitalization values reported in the literature.

nodes.name: Monte Carlo tracking of the parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$
nodes.statement: The values of parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$ were calculated in \cite{[24]} by assuming that all banks of a country are infected; then, using Monte Carlo simulations, the parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$ were tracked for each bank in a country; and aggregated in such a way they represent the average over simulations, with respect to the country in which the bank originates.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate $\beta$ and $\gamma$ per country by Monte Carlo simulation from an all-infected initialization, then average the per-bank values over simulations.

nodes.name: BOCOP time discretization solved by Ipopt with Adol-C derivatives
nodes.statement: The optimal control problem \eqref{eqbocop1}--\eqref{eqbocop2} is approximated by \textsf{BOCOP} into a nonlinear programming problem (NLP) using a standard time discretization. The NLP problem is then solved by the open-source \textsf{Ipopt} optimization solver \cite{ipopt}, using sparse exact derivatives computed by the \textsf{Adol-C} (Automatic Differentiation by OverLoading in \textsf{C++}) package \cite{ADOL-C}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct method: discretize the Mayer-form problem into an NLP with BOCOP, then solve it with Ipopt using Adol-C automatic derivatives.
nodes.origin_citation: Bonnans et al. BOCOP 2015; Wachter & Biegler 2006 (Ipopt); Walther & Griewank 2012 (Adol-C)
output: sparse exact derivatives computed by the \textsf{Adol-C} (Automatic Differentiation by OverLoading in \textsf{C++}) package

nodes.name: Time discretization into an NLP

nodes.statement_short: Solve the NLP with Ipopt using sparse exact derivatives from Adol-C.

nodes.name: Epidemiological models describe bank contagion spread well
nodes.statement: Namely, we show that the application of epidemiological models is able to describe well the nature and character of the contagion spread and its behaviour over time. Our analysis identifies which measures to adopt and when they must be taken in order to prevent effects and serious negative consequences for a particular bank, and for economy as a whole.
nodes.statement_short: Main thesis: epidemic models capture banking contagion, and the analysis says which measures to adopt and when.
conclusions: the application of epidemiological models is able to describe well the nature and character of the contagion spread and its behaviour over time
Our analysis identifies which measures to adopt and when they must be taken in order to prevent effects and serious negative consequences for a particular bank, and for economy as a whole

nodes.name: Condition for a susceptible bank to obtain contagion
nodes.statement: A susceptible bank from group $S$ can obtain contagion if it has a relationship with a contagious bank from group $I$, and if it has not enough money in reserve to cover possible risk losses. In other words, the bank may be contaminated, if it has not enough strong ``health'' in order to resist an epidemic.
nodes.statement_short: A susceptible bank becomes infected when it is exposed to an infected bank and lacks reserves to absorb the losses.
assumptions: it has a relationship with a contagious bank from group $I$
it has not enough money in reserve to cover possible risk losses
conclusions: A susceptible bank from group $S$ can obtain contagion

nodes.name: Scenario-dependent behaviour of contagion and recovery over $T=100$ days
nodes.statement: In the first scenario, contagion spreads rapidly. In a short span of time, contagion reaches its peak and then swiftly decreases. The recovery process takes fast. See Figure~\ref{f2a}. Regarding the second scenario, Figure~\ref{f2b} demonstrates that contamination occurs rapidly as in the first scenario. The contagion affects a large number of banks but the recovery process takes longer. In Figure~\ref{f2c}, we see what happens in the third scenario: the spread of contagion occurs in a longer period of time and, consequently, the recovery process goes slowly too. The graphs of Figure~\ref{f2} show that the processes of contagion take place in different ways, depending on the country where it begins.
nodes.statement_short: Contagion is fast in Portugal and Spain but recovery is slower in Spain, while the UK spreads and recovers slowly --- dynamics depend on the country of origin.

However, $T=100$ is not enough to reach the contagion-free equilibrium for the second and third scenarios. In those cases, it makes sense to increase the time. nodes.statement: As seen from Figure~\ref{f3a}, in case of bank contagion starting in Portugal, less than in half a year the contagion spreading stops. Figure~\ref{f3b} demonstrates that a spreading of contagion starting in Spain will only stop after a full year. The third scenario is the most severe: the contagion will disappear and the banks will be recovered only after three years (see Figure~\ref{f3c}).

nodes.statement: It is worth to mention that the qualitative results of the paper do not change with the particular choice of the weight $b$: the extremal curves change continuously with the change of parameter $b$.

The role of parameter $b$ is more visible in Scenario~3 than in Scenarios 1 and 2.
nodes.statement_short: Larger $b$ penalizes intervention, so the optimal support $u$ decreases --- most visibly in Scenario 3.

nodes.name: Contamination features depend on transmission and recovery rates and on the country of origin
nodes.statement: The features of contamination were shown to depend on the parameter values of the transmission and recovery rates, as well as on the country for which the process of infection begins. The scale of negative consequences for three different scenarios of bank risk contagion were identified.
nodes.statement_short: Contagion behaviour is governed by $\beta$, $\gamma$ and the country where the outbreak starts.
conclusions: The features of contamination were shown to depend on the parameter values of the transmission and recovery rates, as well as on the country for which the process of infection begins
The scale of negative consequences for three different scenarios of bank risk contagion were identified

nodes.name: Financially more influential countries propagate crises more severely
nodes.statement: Banks at risk from countries with greater financial influence in Europe tend to propagate more severely the banking crisis; at the same time, the recovery period is longer.
assumptions: Banks at risk from countries with greater financial influence in Europe
conclusions: tend to propagate more severely the banking crisis
the recovery period is longer

nodes.name: Analogy between financial contagion and disease propagation
nodes.statement: Such processes of contagion in economy are very similar to the disease propagation in a population (from one individual to another). This similarity allows us to consider contagion in such type of financial sectors, as banking, using the same mathematical models of infection spreading as used in epidemiology.
nodes.statement_short: The similarity between financial contagion and disease spread justifies reusing epidemiological models for banking.

nodes.name: The SIR model as a multi-parameter ODE system requiring adaptation to banking
nodes.statement: Mathematically, the SIR model is a multi-parameter system of ordinary differential equations, where each equation defines the current state of health of an investigated object. This model is relevant and frequently used in current research. Our work is also based on its application to the transmission of a contagious disease between banks. The model must be, however, adapted to the banking sector, in order to have a deeper understanding of how the process of infection transmission is carried out, and especially how banks, as financial institutions, become contagious.
nodes.statement_short: The SIR model is a multi-parameter ODE system that must be adapted before it can describe interbank contagion.

nodes.name: Interpretation of the three equations of the model
nodes.statement: The first equation defines the number of banks that leave the group $S$ by becoming a target of market speculation at time $t$; the second equation defines the number of contagious banks at time $t$; and the third equation defines the number of banks that have recovered from the crisis at time $t$, where $t\in [0,T]$, $T > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Each of the three ODEs tracks, respectively, susceptible, contagious and recovered banks at time $t$.

nodes.name: Economic explanation of the differences between scenarios
nodes.statement: The reason behind the differences found, for the three scenarios considered, rely in the different economic relevance, in the global banking market, of the countries where contagion begins. So, if one of the large and important banks of United Kingdom will be the starting point in the spread of contagion, then the global banking market will experience serious problems, the negative effects of which will continue during a long period of time. In other words, United Kingdom is one of the main financial markets to have into account at European level. On the other hand, Portugal has a less powerful and influential economy on an European scale.
nodes.statement_short: The scenario differences trace back to how economically relevant the originating country is in the global banking market.
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data

nodes.name: Role of the Central Bank as supervisory authority
nodes.statement: Given the horizontal linkages in market environment, all banks are equally needed to be under financial supervision. Such supervision is necessary in order to prevent global contamination and avoid serious consequences due to spread of contagion between banks. This partially explains why the Central European Bank exists. The Central Bank is a supervisory competent authority that implements vertical connections among interacting commercial banks.
nodes.statement_short: Supervision by the Central Bank supplies the vertical linkages needed to contain contagion, motivating the control formulation.

nodes.name: Interpretation of the objective functional
nodes.statement: The first term of the objective functional \eqref{eqopt1} reflects the fact that the control organization should take care about the number of contagious institutions $I(T)$ at the final time $T$. The integral represents the general cost of financial assistance necessary to prevent the spread of contagion and economic decline in the period $[0, T]$.
nodes.statement_short: The functional trades off the terminal number of contagious banks $I(T)$ against the accumulated cost of assistance.

nodes.name: Interpretation of the extreme control values $u(t)=1$ and $u(t)=0$
nodes.statement: In this way, $u(t) = 1$ means full support from the Central Bank at time $t$ (all money needed by the banks is being covered by Central Bank), while $u(t) = 0$ means no financial lending or recapitalization from the Central Bank at time $t$.
nodes.statement_short: $u=1$ is full Central Bank coverage of the banks' needs; $u=0$ is no intervention at all.

nodes.name: Differences between the present scenarios and those of Philippas, Koutelidakis and Leontitsis
nodes.statement: Such countries were chosen from \cite{[24]}. However, it should be mentioned that our scenarios are different from those of \cite{[24]}. Indeed, in \cite{[24]} they begin with one or more random banks among three different levels of assets. In contrast, here we do not look to the assets level of the banks and, instead, we chose countries by their contagion and recovery rates, respectively $\beta$ and $\gamma$. Moreover, in our cases all the three scenarios begin with exactly one random infected bank in the chosen country, while in \cite{[24]} more than one is allowed.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike the source study, scenarios here are selected by $\beta$ and $\gamma$ rather than asset level, and start from exactly one infected bank.
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data

nodes.name: Optimal control problem for bank contagion (Bolza form)
nodes.statement: Since one of the main goals is to avoid the wide dissemination of a contagion, we pose the following optimal control problem: \begin{equation} \min \mathcal{J}[I(\cdot),u(\cdot)] =I(T)+\int\limits_0^T b u^2(t) dt \longrightarrow \min \end{equation} subject to the control system \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{dS(t)}{dt} = - \beta S(t) I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dI(t)}{dt} = \beta S(t) I(t) - \gamma I(t)-u(t)I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dR(t)}{dt} = \gamma I(t)+u(t)I(t), \end{cases} \end{equation} where $S(0) = S_0$, $I(0) = I_0$, $R(0) = R_0$, satisfying \eqref{eq:IC:assump}, and the weight $b > 0$, are fixed.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $I(T)+\int_0^T b u^2(t)\,dt$ over $u(\cdot)$ subject to the controlled SIR dynamics with fixed initial conditions and $b>0$.

nodes.name: Mayer form of the optimal control problem
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \min \mathcal{J}[S(\cdot),R(\cdot),Y(\cdot)] =N-S(T)-R(T)+Y(T)\longrightarrow \min \end{equation} subject to \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{dS(t)}{dt} = \beta S^2(t)+ \beta S(t)(R(t)-N),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dR(t)}{dt} = \gamma (N-S(t)-R(t))+u(t)(N-S(t)-R(t)),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dY(t)}{dt} = bu^2(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle S(0)=S_0, \quad R(0)=0, \quad Y(0)=0,\\[0.3cm] u(t) \in [0, 1]. \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The same problem in Mayer form: minimize $N-S(T)-R(T)+Y(T)$ with the cost accumulated in the extra state $Y$.
